items.stem:
DOCUMENT-BASED QUESTION: The Space Race — Science, Security, and Superpower Prestige

Directions: Read the following two primary source excerpts and respond to the prompt below. Apply SOAPS analysis to both documents and construct an evidence-based argument.

---
DOCUMENT A: President Dwight D. Eisenhower, Statement on the Sputnik Launch, October 9, 1957 — press conference transcript, available through the Dwight D. Eisenhower Presidential Library (National Archives):
"The Soviets have put one small ball in the air... Now so far as the satellite itself is concerned, that does not raise my apprehensions, not one iota. I see nothing at this moment, at this stage of development, that is significant in that development as far as security is concerned... So far as I know, the [Soviet satellite] has added nothing to [their] military capabilities."

DOCUMENT B: President John F. Kennedy, Special Message to Congress on Urgent National Needs, May 25, 1961 — U.S. government document, available through the John F. Kennedy Presidential Library (National Archives):
"I believe that this Nation should commit itself to achieving the goal, before this decade is out, of landing a man on the Moon and returning him safely to the Earth. No single space project in this period will be more impressive to mankind, or more important for the long-range exploration of space; and none will be so difficult or expensive to accomplish."

---
Using both documents and your knowledge of the Space Race (US.65, US.67), construct an argument that evaluates the Space Race as a strategic competition beyond its scientific dimensions. Apply SOAPS analysis to both documents and address: (1) what the contrast between Eisenhower's and Kennedy's responses reveals about how the political meaning of the Space Race evolved; (2) how the Space Race connected to the military-industrial complex and defense spending (US.67); and (3) whether the Space Race was primarily about military security, national prestige, or ideological demonstration — and what evidence supports your position.
items.stemEs:
PREGUNTA BASADA EN DOCUMENTOS: La Carrera Espacial — Ciencia, Seguridad y Prestigio de las Superpotencias

Instrucciones: Lee los siguientes dos fragmentos de fuentes primarias y responde al indicador. Aplica el análisis SOAPS a ambos documentos.

DOCUMENTO A: Presidente Dwight D. Eisenhower, Declaración sobre el Lanzamiento del Sputnik, 9 de octubre de 1957.
"Los soviéticos han puesto una pequeña bola en el aire... En cuanto al satélite en sí, eso no aumenta mis aprensiones, ni un ápice..."

DOCUMENTO B: Presidente John F. Kennedy, Mensaje Especial al Congreso sobre Necesidades Nacionales Urgentes, 25 de mayo de 1961.
"Creo que esta Nación debería comprometerse a lograr el objetivo, antes de que termine esta década, de aterrizar a un hombre en la Luna y regresarlo sano y salvo a la Tierra."

Usando ambos documentos y tu conocimiento de la Carrera Espacial (US.65, US.67), construye un argumento que evalúe la Carrera Espacial como una competencia estratégica más allá de sus dimensiones científicas.
items.correctAnswer: A top-scoring (6/6) response would include: THESIS — A precise, arguable thesis (e.g., 'The Space Race was fundamentally an ideological demonstration of superpower technological capability that was inseparable from military competition, as shown by the transformation of U.S. space policy from Eisenhower's calculated calm to Kennedy's existential commitment after Soviet achievements made ideological stakes undeniable'). SOAPS ANALYSIS: Document A — Speaker: President Eisenhower, a military commander who understood both the technical and strategic dimensions of missile technology; Occasion: Press conference days after Sputnik launch on October 4, 1957 — the first artificial satellite, demonstrating Soviet ICBM-range delivery capability; Audience: American press, public, and indirectly Soviet leadership; Purpose: To prevent public panic and downplay Sputnik's security implications; Significance: Eisenhower's strategic calm was partially genuine (U.S. intelligence via U-2 overflights already knew Soviet capabilities) and partially political — he did not want to escalate defense spending further or acknowledge the psychological blow. His restraint was later seen as a political miscalculation. Document B — Speaker: President Kennedy, 4 months after his inauguration, following Soviet cosmonaut Yuri Gagarin's orbit (April 12, 1961) and the Bay of Pigs fiasco; Occasion: Special Message to Congress, framed as a national security and prestige emergency; Audience: Congress and the American public; Purpose: To commit the nation to a defined, achievable Space Race goal that the U.S. could win; Significance: Kennedy chose the Moon specifically because the Soviets had not yet announced it as a goal — selecting a competition the U.S. could win rather than one already lost. OUTSIDE EVIDENCE: Sputnik's actual military significance (demonstrated ICBM-range rocket capability); National Defense Education Act (1958) as educational response; NASA creation (1958) as institutional response; Vostok 1 (Gagarin, April 1961); Apollo 11 Moon landing (July 20, 1969); Apollo program's $25 billion cost and workforce of 400,000.
items.dokRationale: Student must synthesize across multiple standards and sources, constructing an extended argument that connects US.65, US.67 through evidence-based reasoning requiring sustained analytical writing.
items.explanation:
SCORING GUIDE (6 points):
6 - Exemplary: Precise, arguable thesis on the Space Race's strategic/ideological significance. Full SOAPS on both documents (all 5 elements, historically accurate, including Eisenhower's strategic reasons for calm and Kennedy's competitive selection logic). Outside evidence (minimum 3 specific facts). Addresses all three prompt components. Synthesizes the contrast between documents to reveal evolving U.S. strategic posture.
5 - Advanced: Clear thesis. Full SOAPS on both documents (may miss one element). Two outside evidence points. Addresses two of three prompt components.
4 - Proficient: Arguable thesis. SOAPS partially applied to both documents. One outside evidence fact. Addresses two prompt components.
3 - Adequate: General thesis. Analyzes both documents without systematic SOAPS. Some outside knowledge.
2 - Developing: Basic claim. References documents, mostly summary.
1 - Beginning: Attempts a response without substantive analysis.
0 - No response or off-topic.

DOCUMENT ANALYSIS EXPECTATIONS: Document A SOAPS — the gap between Eisenhower's public calm and private U-2 intelligence knowledge; the military-industrial complex context of his warning in 1961 as connected to NASA's establishment. Document B SOAPS — Kennedy's selection of the Moon as a strategic choice to define a winnable competition; the $25 billion commitment as the MIC in action.
KEY EVIDENCE EXPECTED: Sputnik launch (Oct. 4, 1957); ICBM implications; National Defense Education Act (1958); NASA creation (1958); Gagarin orbit (April 12, 1961); Bay of Pigs failure (April 1961) as Kennedy's motivation context; Apollo 11 (July 20, 1969); total Apollo program cost (~$25 billion).
items.explanationEs:
GUÍA DE PUNTUACIÓN (6 puntos):
6 - Ejemplar: Tesis precisa y argumentable sobre la importancia estratégica/ideológica de la Carrera Espacial. SOAPS completo en ambos documentos. Evidencia externa (mínimo 3 hechos específicos). Aborda los tres componentes del indicador.
5 - Avanzado: Tesis clara. SOAPS completo en ambos documentos. Dos puntos de evidencia externa.
4 - Competente: Tesis argumentable. SOAPS parcialmente aplicado. Un hecho de evidencia externa específica.
3 - Adecuado: Tesis general. Analiza ambos documentos sin SOAPS sistemático.
2 - En desarrollo: Afirmación básica. Referencias a documentos, principalmente resumen.
1 - Inicial: Intenta una respuesta sin análisis sustantivo.
0 - Sin respuesta o fuera del tema.

EVIDENCIA CLAVE ESPERADA: Lanzamiento del Sputnik (4 de oct. de 1957); implicaciones del ICBM; Ley de Educación para la Defensa Nacional (1958); creación de la NASA (1958); órbita de Gagarin (12 de abril de 1961); Apollo 11 (20 de julio de 1969); costo total del programa Apollo (~$25 mil millones).
